title: 2.4.26 Plain English to Pseudocode: Nested Loops
description: Turn plain-English steps into pseudocode for a row/col nested loop: the inner loop starts over for every round of the outer loop.
sourceRef: designed: extends the single-hexagon pattern from module 2.2's 'Chart the for-loop' to two nested hexagons for book 2.4.6

planChart.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A([the program starts]) --> B{{row = 1 to 3}}
  B -- next row --> C{{col = 1 to 4}}
  C -- next col --> D[/print row and col/]
  D --> C
  C -- inner done --> B

planChart.caption: Two hexagons, one inside the other: the print goes back to the INNER hexagon, and only when the inner one is done does flow return to the OUTER one.

steps.title: Turn the plain-English steps into pseudocode
steps.instructions:
Here is the plan in plain English:

**1.** For each `row` from `1` to `3`, do steps 2 and 3.

**2.** Inside that: for each `col` from `1` to `4`, print `row` and `col` (for example `row 1, col 1`).

**3.** When the `col` loop has finished all four values, the `row` loop moves on to its next `row`, and the `col` loop starts again from `1`.

The same plan is drawn as a flow chart above the editor (open the Flow Chart bar). You do not draw it, you read it: two hexagons, the print goes back to the inner one, and only a finished inner loop returns to the outer one.

In `README.md`, type these as numbered pseudocode **between the first and last line**. Number every line, including indented ones, and indent the inner loop under the outer one. Each keyword looks like this, in a different program:

- `FOR EACH a FROM 1 TO 2` ... `END FOR` (a loop, the steps inside indented)
- a second `FOR EACH b FROM 1 TO 5` indented inside it, with its own `END FOR`
- `PRINT a` (show something)

Plain English is fine. Press **Grade** above the editor: the AI reads what your steps mean and marks each Quest card green or red. Changing your text clears its marks, so press Grade again when you have finished editing.

Before you submit, trace `row 1` by hand: it prints col 1, 2, 3, 4, and only then does `row 2` begin. In all, 3 x 4 = 12 lines print.
hints: The inner loop sits inside the outer loop, so indent it one level more and close it first.
Print both values: the line says which row and which col.

requirements.title: Numbered steps
requirements.description: Number your steps 1. 2. 3. and so on, with something written after each number.
requirements.hint: Write at least four lines that start with a number, each with a step written after it.

requirements.title: The outer loop is row, 1 to 3
requirements.description: A loop step that goes through row from 1 to 3.
requirements.hint: Add a loop step: for each row from 1 to 3.

requirements.title: The inner loop is col, 1 to 4
requirements.description: A loop step that goes through col from 1 to 4.
requirements.hint: Add a loop step: for each col from 1 to 4.

requirements.title: The col loop sits inside the row loop
requirements.description: The col loop starts after the row loop starts and finishes before it does, so it restarts for every row.
requirements.hint: Indent the col loop under the row loop and close it before you close the row loop.

requirements.title: The print is inside the col loop
requirements.description: The print is a step of the inner loop, so it happens for every col in every row.
requirements.hint: Put the print between the col loop opening and its END FOR.

requirements.title: The print shows both row and col
requirements.description: Each printed line says which row and which col it is.
requirements.hint: Print the row and the col together, e.g. "row 1, col 1".

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your steps
aiCheck.prompt: The student was given plain-English steps and rewrote them as numbered, step-by-step pseudocode in README.md, between a first line and a last line that were already there. The program is: for (let row = 1; row <= 3; row++) { for (let col = 1; col <= 4; col++) { console.log("row " + row + ", col " + col); } }. It prints 12 lines. The point: the col loop is INSIDE the row loop and starts over for every row; the print is inside the col loop; the row only moves on after the col loop has finished. Judge each criterion ONLY by whether its idea is present in the student's steps, however they word it. Plain English, keywords such as SET, IF, ELSE, END IF, FOR EACH, END FOR, CALL, PRINT, or a mix of both are all fine, and so are different names, different capitalisation, and different ways to number the lines. Do not require any particular keyword. A step that is clearly aimed at the criterion is enough for 'met'. Mark a criterion 'missing' only when the idea is absent or the steps do the opposite (for example the col loop placed after the row loop instead of inside it, or the print placed outside the col loop). Write each note for THIS student's own steps: in a not-met note, name the exact step or word in their steps that causes the problem (quote at most a few words), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected steps. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their steps satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.

rubric.title: Numbered steps
rubric.description: The student numbered their steps (1. 2. 3. or similar), at least four of them.

rubric.title: The outer loop is row, 1 to 3
rubric.description: A loop step that goes through row from 1 to 3.

rubric.title: The inner loop is col, 1 to 4
rubric.description: A loop step that goes through col from 1 to 4.

rubric.title: The col loop sits inside the row loop
rubric.description: The col loop is NESTED inside the row loop: it starts after the row loop starts and is finished before the row loop is finished, so it runs again for every row. Two loops one after the other (the row loop closed before the col loop opens) do NOT meet this.

rubric.title: The print is inside the col loop
rubric.description: The print is a step INSIDE the col loop (before the col loop is closed), so it runs for every col of every row. A print placed after the col loop has closed runs only once per row.

rubric.title: The print shows both row and col
rubric.description: The printed line shows BOTH the row and the col (like "row 1, col 1"). Printing only one of them does not meet this.
